items.title: This Opensource Repo Actually saves upto 98% USAGE across Codex,Claude & More!?
items.summary:
Join this channel to get access to perks:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/@aicodeking/join

In this video, I'll take a look at pxpipe, an open-source local proxy that cuts coding agent input tokens by rendering bulky text context into dense 5x8 pixel page images. I'll explain why image token math beats raw text on dense code and JSON, what the proxy compresses versus leaves alone, and the headline end-to-end bill savings, session demo, and SWE-bench results. Next, I'll break down the part that matters most—which models can actually read 5x8 pixel text cleanly like Gemini 4 and Gemini Flash versus gist readers like Opus 5.5 or models you should not image at all—plus silent confabulations and the text factsheet fix. Finally, I'll show how to run npx pxpipe-proxy, put Claude Code, the Antigravity CLI, OpenCode, Codex, and omp behind pxpipe warp, use the dashboard, offline export, and pxpipe stats, and decide whether it's worth using.

--

items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi, welcome to another video. So there is a project on GitHub called PX Pipe that has been getting a lot of attention lately. It sits at around 7,600 stars. It is MIT licensed and the idea behind it sounds a bit crazy at first. It cuts the input tokens of your coding agent by turning the bulky text in your context into images. Now, why would that save anything? Well, the cost of an image is set by its pixel size, not by how much text you put inside it. A normal text token holds about one character of dense code or JSON, but on real Claude code traffic, one image token holds about 3.1 characters of the same stuff. So if you print your system prompt and tool docs onto a dense page and send the page instead, you pay for far fewer tokens. And this is not a small difference. In their example, about 48,000 characters of system prompt and tool docs come to roughly 25,000 tokens as text. The same content as one rendered page is about 2.7,000 image tokens. This is what the model actually sees. It is a page of 25 by eight pixel letters with a banner on top and a little arrow wherever the original had a new line. So how does it work? PX Pipe is a local proxy that runs on your machine. Your agent sends its request. PX Pipe rewrites the heavy parts into PNG pages and then the request goes on to the provider. It only touches the request. The response from the model streams back as normal text, so nothing changes on the output side. It also does not image everything. It picks three kinds of input. The first is the big static block of system prompt and tool docs. The second is large tool results like file reads and long command output above roughly 6,000 characters. And the third is older chat history. Your recent turns always stay as text and so do your own messages. Now, the headline numbers on the original Claude Fable 5 from June, they measured a 59 to 70% lower bill end-to-end. And end-to-end means the whole bill here, including output tokens and cash reads that the proxy never compresses. They also have a demo with plain Claude code on the left and PX pipe on the right doing the same task. The plain session ends at about $42 with the context 96% full. PX pipe session ends at about $6 with the context at only 73,000 out of 1 million. So that's kind of awesome. They also ran it on Steer UE Bench. On Steer UE Bench Light, both arms solved 10 out of 10 tasks and the PX pipe arms sent 65% less per request. On Steer UE Bench Pro, PX pipe got 14 out of 19 and Plain Text got 15 out of 19 at 60% less. That is a small sample and they say so themselves, but it shows the model still does real work while it reads its history from pictures and the savings are not guessed. For every request, the proxy also sends the original uncompressed body to the free count tokens endpoint and then it compares that with what you were actually billed. Both numbers go into one events file in your home folder so you can check the math on your own usage. Now let's talk about the part that matters most, which is which models can actually read this. And this is where the README is surprisingly honest. Not every model can read dense 5 by 8 pixel text. Their main test hides 15 random hex IDs in log images and asks the model to read them back exactly. Gemini 4 Argon gets all 15. Gemini 3.6 to 3.8 Flash got 14. The original Fable 5 gets 13, but the newer Claude models went backwards here. Opus 5.5 gets only 3 out of 15 and Sonnet 5.5 gets 2. Fable 5.1 and 5.2 also dropped, but PX pipe adds 2 pixels of spacing between rows for them and that brings them back up to 14 and 13. So the render settings change per model, which is a good touch. Because of this, they sort models into tiers. Gemini 4, Gemini Flash, and the original Fable 5 are full readers. Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 and 5.2 are what they call gist readers. They understand what the history is about and they do fine on arithmetic, but you should not trust them with exact IDs or numbers from an image. And then there is a list of models they say not to image at all, which includes Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, GPT 6 Astra, Kimi K3, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. So, what happens when a weak reader gets an image it cannot read? It does not throw an error. It just makes up something that looks right. The README even says this happened once in weeks of real use where the model recalled a person's name from image chat history and got it confidently wrong. The reason is that model vision is not OCR. The model never sees discrete letters. So, when the pixels are unclear, it fills the gap with a likely guess. They found a nice example of this, too. In this font, a zero and an eight differ by a single pixel. So, even Gemini 4 sometimes read a zero in a request ID as an eight. To fix this, PX Pipe sends a small text factsheet next to the image with the exact IDs and numbers, and the model uses it to check what it reads. So, there's that. In coding sessions, this is less of a problem because the agent usually reads a file again before it edits it. But if you use it for pure chat recall or for pulling exact values out of logs, you should keep this in mind. Now, let's look at how you actually use it. To start it, you just run NPX PX Pipe - proxy. That starts the proxy on port 47821 on your local machine, and the same address gives you a dashboard. Then, to put an agent behind it, you use the warp command. You run PX Pipe Warp then - - then the agent's command. So, PX Pipe Warp - - Claude for Claude code, PX Pipe Warp - - AGI for the Antigravity CLI, or PX Pipe Warp - - Open Code for Open Code. It also works with Codex and OMP. The nice thing about warp is that you do not change any base URL. It only diverts the specific provider routes. So, things like the OAuth login in AG or remote control and connectors in Claude Code keep working. And if your agent talks to a custom gateway on some local port, you can add a - - route rule for that port. The dashboard is quite good as well. It shows the tokens you saved, every text to image conversion side by side, so you can see exactly what got imaged. Chips to turn individual models on or off in a kill switch. By default, it images Fable 5, Opus 5.5, and every Gemini model. If you do not want Opus imaged, you can just click its chip off or set the PX Pipe Models variable to only the models you trust. There is also an escape hatch for exact work. Sub-agents on models that are not on the list pass through as plain text, so you can send the byte exact jobs to a sub-agent on a model like Sonnet 4.6 and keep the big main session imaged. And if you do not want a proxy at all, there is an offline export. You run NPX PxPipe-proxy export and then give it a folder like SRC. It writes a fresh folder with the page images, the fact sheet, a manifest, and a prompt file. You can also pipe text into it with dash-dash-CDN or export your current git diff with dash-dash-git. Then you can upload those pages to any tool that takes images like Cursor and paste the prompt with them. When you're done, PxPipe stats reads that events file and prints a report of your requests, compression, latency, and cache hits with the measured savings at the top. And this works even when the proxy is not running. Now, I want to mention a few more things. It handles Anthropic messages, the OpenAI responses, and chat completions formats and Google's generate content requests. On Anthropic, it keeps the prompt cache boundary in place. That matters a lot because if the images changed on every turn, you would lose your cache discount and pay more, not less. And one funny detail, the FAQ asks why the README reads like an AI wrote it. And the answer is that one did. Most of the commits in this repo came from Opus and Fable sessions that ran behind PxPipe itself, reading their own history as images while they worked. So should you use it? If you're on Gemini 4 or Gemini Flash, I think this is a really good option for sure because those models read the pages almost perfectly and the savings are big. If you're on the original Fable 5, same thing. If you're on Opus 5.5, it can still save you money in a normal coding session where the agent has tools to read files again, but I would not use it for work where exact strings matter. And if you're on Sonnet, Haiku, or most of the open models, the project itself tells you not to bother yet. The other thing I like is that it is open about where it fails. Most token saving tools only show you the savings on the part they touched And PX pipe shows the whole bill and a full table of the models that cannot read its output. The downsides are that it adds a bit of latency while it encodes the PNGs. And that the model list keeps moving, so a model that reads well today can get worse in the next release, like Opus 5.5 did. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking [music] the Join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.
